comment: I am writing as a concerned member of the community regarding the issue of tennis court availability. My husband has been a part of Park City since the 80s and we have been here with our daughters for last 7 years. I spent 4 years being the team mom for the PCHS tennis team that my husband helped coach, I have captained and still am currently captaining multiple teams out of the MARC (one of which is about to go represent our city/facility competing in Nationals in FL), I take private lessons, attend clinics and have had my kids do tennis lessons/clinics as well. Since we have such a large population of tennis players in the community, it has been difficult to book a court because they are in such high demand. This is about to get a lot worse when the outdoor courts are no longer available. It is nearly impossible to get tennis courts during the winter. If we start giving pickleball players more court time, this is going to severely impact our ability to play. How can we create a team strong enough to compete in something like Nationals if we can’t get our team time on the court together to play? There are multiple tennis facilities in Salt Lake that are not allowing pickleball players to bully their way into more court time. Salt Lake Tennis club, Liberty Park, Sports Mall, Wasatch Hills, Ivory Ridge, Eagle Ridge, Eccles Tennis Center….and I know there are more that I’m not thinking of off the top of my head. Some of these are private clubs but at least a couple are public facilities like the MARC. A lot of these facilities even have more indoor courts available than the MARC and they still aren’t designating any of them to be used by pickleball players. And when you think about the options just in the Salt Lake area for indoor courts, it makes our 7 courts look like nothing. So if you are going to take the only 7 courts in all of Summit County and take even more of that away from the tennis community, it seems really unfair. A lot of the tennis players in this community have been loyal to the MARC for many years, if not decades. Pickleball players have a lot more options for surfaces where they can play. Tennis players do not have that luxury. We as tennis players should not have to defend ourselves to be able to play tennis on the court it was intended to be played on. To me, it’s absolutely absurd that we have to continually fight about this issue. If the pickleball players feel so strongly about their ability to play, then they need to utilize the other surface options available for them to play on and/or band together to build a facility designated for pickleball somewhere in Summit County. If you give in to this request to take away even more from the tennis players, it will show the community that you really don’t care about the dozens of opinions on this issue. In a sense, you are robbing Peter to pay Paul. My question is: why are the pickleball players that have just come around in the last couple years so much more important to the council than the tennis pros at the MARC and/or the tennis patrons that have been a long-standing part of this community?

comment: I am emailing regarding the discussion (and vote?) tomorrow on the use of tennis courts. I am concerned as I love tennis and it's increasingly VERY difficult to find tennis court time in Park City. While the tennis community is not as organized as the pickleball community, there is INSUFFICIENT existing court time available for tennis, winter and summer. I understand Pickleball players want to play. Taking exclusively from tennis courts is arbitrary and unfair. Pickleball can be played on basketball courts (the courts at Willow Creek don't seem to be used often), parking lots, or any flat surface. Taking **MORE** time from tennis courts is unfair and arbitrary. I tried to take my son to play tennis on a Saturday morning and tennis courts were already occupied by pickleball (!!!) so we could not play. These were purpose-built TENNIS courts. If we need Pickleball facilities, the city should consider construction (I voted for the last bill which didn't pass) but the solution is not to take away heavily used tennis facilities. Lacrosse is picking up in popularity and some new fields have been built - we have not simply cancelled soccer and taken away the facilities from soccer players. I do not play golf on the rugby field!

comment: As a member of the tennis community, business owner and resident of Park City, I am writing to urge you to keep the tennis courts solely tennis courts. I am a pickle ball player as well but pickle ball lines are very disruptive on the court when playing tennis. Pickle ball is much better as well when playing on dedicated pickle ball courts. I am surprised that the pickle ball community does not convert a large space such as the Bed Bath and Beyond into a dedicated facility. Most communities are doing such things. I do not know any municipal or private entity who has made the solution of combining tennis and pickle as a positive way forward. They are separate games and need their own designated courts. This is a great franchise that a resident who values pickle should consider developing, https://chickennpickle.com /location/san-antonio/.

comment: I'm writing to offer my opinion on the pending discussion concerning significantly reallocating court time from tennis to pickleball ("PB") at the PC Marc. My wife and I have been full time residents of Park City for 15 years, and in that period the availability of court time for tennis, especially in the winter when the population of Park City surges, has declined significantly. Scheduling court time now requires planning days in advance and clinics are almost always significantly oversubscribed. This has worsened in the last two years as more court time has been "dedicated" to pickleball. While the long standing tennis community may have grumbled about the loss of court time, we adjusted in a spirit of accommodation. At the same time, the PB community has become increasingly strident in what are basically demands to take the tennis courts from tennis and give them over to PB. In what universe is it appropriate to simply take away a long standing resource from one group of citizens and give it to another? And why are these discussions not being more widely publicized? Was there notice of this meeting posted in the MARC, where the tennis community could see it and respond? No. There was not. Please don't unilaterally destroy one community in favor of another. Make the tough decision to build dedicated PB facilities; bubble the extra outdoor courts at the MARC for exclusive use of PB. Introduce differential pricing for residents of Park City versus those using the courts from other geographies to reserve this asset for city residents first. In the short run, there is no easy solution, but unilaterally slashing tennis court time is inappropriate and unfair. Thank you for your consideration and for your service to the City.

comment: It has come to my attention that the current time allotted for playing tennis on the tennis courts at the MARC (and maybe on all Park City tennis courts) will be reduced. I love playing tennis in Park City. I am amazed by the number of players who enjoy the sport not only in this area, but also in the world. Please do not take away any time that is available for playing tennis in Park City. The programs are strong. The rate for court times is reasonable. People of all ages, from youth to senior citizen, and all abilities, from absolute beginner to pro, are found on the courts. School teams and USTA League teams often qualify for district, regional and national competitions. All of this is only possible if people have access to court time. As it is, because of the enthusiasm for tennis in Park City, it can be a challenge to find available courts. I urge you not to cut back on any court time and to keep the tennis courts for playing tennis.

comment: The results of this process, RAB and Court Allocation Subcommittee, were not shared with the MARC tennis and pickleball community. Cole Johnston's letter to the City Council is the first we have heard of the recommendations. I would respectfully ask members of City Council and Mayor Nann Worel to take public input at a future meeting. However, I do not approve of the MARC Tennis & Operational plan as presented by Cole Johnston and apparently supported by the RAB and the Court Allocation Subcommittee. I am asking City Council not to move forward on this recommendation. The schedule being considered will convert half of the tennis courts to pickleball courts, during the indoor season. It is already a challenge for tennis players to get court time during the winter. Pickleball will now take more of this court time. Many of the SLC tennis centers are not opening up to Pickleball players. Also, many pickleball players are coming from outside Park City and are demanding that we accommodate them with indoor courts. We still have a healthy vibrant tennis community….we do not want to destroy it. I am a Park City resident (84060) and active tennis players for 19 years.

comment: There is word spreading through the tennis community now about a city council meeting tomorrow evening where you will be discussing the possibility of taking additional indoor court time away from tennis players at the MARC this winter and giving it to pickle ball players. Possibly as much as 25% more, which is in addition to the court time that was given to pickle ball players last winter. I have been a life long tennis player and am now also a part time tennis instructor at the MARC. I am teaching a beginners tennis clinic tomorrow evening at the MARC so I will unfortunately not be able to attend the meeting, but I would like to provide my input for you to consider. And I have cc’d all of the tennis players that were on the group email I received this morning that mentioned tomorrow’s meeting so that they can provide additional, or other input, they may have on the matter. These are my thoughts and ideas: I know that pickle ball is a popular and fun sport and that there is a shortage of pickle ball courts in Park City. But tennis is also popular. Taking away tennis courts and giving them to pickle ball players is not a valid solution. It just makes the large, but currently less vocal, tennis community upset. In my opinion, all 7 current indoor courts at the MARC (the 4 in the main building and the 3 in the bubble) should be used 100 percent for tennis this fall and winter. There are more than enough tennis players, leagues, clinics and lessons to fill up all 7 courts for tennis use. And to accommodate the demand for pickle ball, the city should consider a few different options: 1. Put another bubble, or bubbles, over tennis courts 5,6,10 and 11. These are the summer tennis courts that currently do not have a bubble over them in the winter. And/or put a bubble over the 4 outdoor pickle ball courts at the MARC. All of those courts would then be used solely for pickle ball. 2. Put a bubble over the 3 outdoor tennis courts at City Park and use them for pickle ball this winter. In a city that has as much money as Park City, there is no reason one, or all of these things, cannot be done and done quickly. And for a future looking solution to the problem, I think more pickle ball and tennis courts need to be built in the Park City area. About six months ago, I emailed the Mayor and City Council members with the following idea, which I feel is still a very good approach: An indoor/outdoor tennis and pickleball facility should be built at the Treasure Mountain Junior High School site. The high school teams and gym classes would get priority using them and the public can use them at other times. I anticipate pickle ball will become a school sport in the future, so this is a way to get ahead of the game. The Junior High School will no longer be used for grades 8 and 9 starting next school year, so I think this would be a great use of a bit of the land there for the school district and for the community. If there is any money left over or set aside for Treasure Mountain usage from the large school bond that was passed, then this is how the construction would be paid for. If no money remains from it, then it can be funded in other ways. Follow Up - I have cc’d the tennis community, again, plus a few more people, on this email so they are informed on my new research, and so they can provide additional comments to you. I do not have the email addresses of the pickleball players who have an interest in this matter, so someone please forward this email along to them. I will not cc everyone like this again in the future since I know large cc’s are sometimes not appreciated by the recipients. The email I sent last week offered a few ideas I had on achieving a situation in which pickleball players have courts of their own to use exclusively this winter and where the tennis community has all seven (four indoor and three bubble) courts available solely for use for tennis this winter, as had been done in the years prior to the rise in popularity of pickleball. Ed from the City Council was kind enough to respond to my prior email with some insight into reasons why it is difficult to make this situation happen (his reply is below, as well). I am now going to proceed being inspired by what I learned from watching my daughter, who was a member of the state champion Park City High School Debate Team last year, prepare for events. The team would research a topic, understand the different sides of it and then present what they think is the best solution. So….Last Friday, I briefly saw Ken Fisher near the bubble and I asked him if it would be possible to put up another structure to cover additional outdoor courts at the MARC this winter so they could be used exclusively for pickleball (courts 5 and 6 or courts 10 and 11) as well as the two pickleball courts that are adjacent to them. In this scenario, pickleball would have the equivalent of 6 pickleball courts to use every hour, 7 days a week. That would be more time than they would have in the bubble this winter which is now the source of conflict. Ken said he had already asked the company that constructed the bubble if this was possible and that company told him they thought it would not be feasible. So I asked Ken if it would be OK for me to do a bit of research on the matter and he said “yes”. I believe I have located a company that can do this. It is named Allsite Structures. They have put up temporary structures for sports venues around the world that are located in all weather conditions. I sent an aerial photo and ground level photos of the outdoor courts at PC MARC for them to review and I spoke to one of their sales reps and to their in-house sports specialist. The structure they provide is different than a bubble. The bubble uses blowing air to stay inflated. The new structure would be a metal frame covered with insulated fabric. Their specialist does not think there would be any technical issues in having a bubble and their structure side by side. She mentioned that snow would need to be cleared from the walkway separating the structures in a prompt manner. Over the phone, I was told the ballpark cost for Allsite Structures to put up and take down a temporary structure that covers two additional tennis courts and the two pickleball courts is $60,000-70,000 for the structure. Plus, another $30,000 to purchase the lighting, which they install, as well. It may be possible to rent the lighting for a bit less. They do not set up HVAC within the structure, but they can consult with a company that Park City hires to do it so that the specifications, etc., are correct. It would take Allsite 10 days to construct. From Ed’s email, the Park City Planning Board would have to sign off on it, too. I imagine there may be some issues with the adjacent condos. Perhaps if the Mayor, the City Council, the tennis and the pickleball communities were strongly if favor of this proposal, then the Planning Board would be more inclined to pass it and to do so in a rapid fashion. No doubt, there would be additional costs – some which are obvious (insurance, etc.) and some which are not obvious. Perhaps a majority of the costs would be recuperated by the strong demand for court usage by the pickleball community. Perhaps additional funding, if needed, can be obtained through sponsorships from individuals and/or companies. And/or perhaps the City would conclude that absorbing a portion of the cost, if necessary, would be a worthy endeavor if it makes the MARC community happy and enthusiastic instead of discontent. This type of structure is not unprecedented and so I think any unpredicted obstacles in constructing it, taking it down, etc. can be resolved. According to Ed, a permanent pickleball facility will not be available until the summer of 2026 at the earliest, so this is one potential way to appease the tennis and pickleball communities this winter, as well as next winter. If there is a will to do so in Park City, then this is possibly a way. I will pass along the contact information for the people I have spoken with at Allsite Structures to Ken Fisher so he can follow up with them, if desired, with additional questions to see if it is truly feasible.
